2025 was the year Hollywood decided subtlety was a liability. Our database captured 135 films and shows from the calendar year, and the ideological signature was unmistakable: two STRONGLY WOKE entries, seven WOKE, and sixteen WOKE LEAN -- not a single neutral or traditionally leaning title cracked the top 25. The range ran from Zootopia 2's staggering -38.40 margin to One Battle After Another's modest -4.00. The median: roughly -6.80, a full WOKE LEAN on a film that is just average for its year.

What made 2025 distinctive was the distribution. Ideology did not concentrate in prestige dramas the way it did in 2024. It spread everywhere. Animation delivered the most woke film of the year. Horror produced three entries in the top ten. Netflix and Disney competed for ideological dominance with multiple series each. Ari Aster, Yorgos Lanthimos, James Cameron, Steven Soderbergh, and Paul Thomas Anderson all released films on this list -- the auteurs were as ideologically committed as the franchises. The walls between entertainment and advocacy did not thin in 2025. They collapsed.

Several films on this list were box-office disasters. Snow White lost over $60 million. Tron: Ares grossed $142 million against a $220 million budget. The Electric State cost $320 million and earned a 14% Rotten Tomatoes score. Audiences are not rejecting these films out of political consciousness -- they are rejecting them because ideological messaging has become a reliable signal that story and craft took a back seat. The market is speaking. Hollywood is not yet listening. Ranked from most woke to least woke.

STRONGLY WOKE (Margin -20 and Below)

#1: Zootopia 2 (2025)

Woke Score: 91.4 • Traditional Score: 53 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -38.40

Zootopia 2 is both the most woke film of 2025 and the best-made film on this list, which is precisely what makes it dangerous. Disney's sequel takes the original's allegorical framework and dials it up: systemic exclusion, historical revisionism, and colonial theft are the load-bearing structure of the plot. The Lynxley family built their dynasty on stolen reptile architecture and manufactured anti-reptile hysteria. The marginalized community has a hidden genius whose work was stolen. These are standard progressive frameworks, delivered with unambiguous clarity. And yet -- Judy Hopps and Nick Wilde are police officers who are heroes, brave and self-sacrificing. The resolution is achieved through evidence and legal process, not destruction of the system. The partnership at the film's heart is built on earned trust and demonstrated loyalty. Zootopia 2 proves that craft can make ideology palatable, which is exactly why conservative viewers need to watch it and talk about it afterward. At -38.40, it is the most ideologically aggressive film of 2025.

#2: Bugonia (2025)

Woke Score: 28.94 • Traditional Score: 8.48 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: -20.46

Yorgos Lanthimos made a beautifully crafted, darkly funny vehicle for the proposition that humanity deserves extinction. Bugonia follows two conspiracy-obsessed men who kidnap a pharmaceutical CEO (Emma Stone, shaving her head for the role) convinced she is an alien overlord. The film's final twist confirms she actually is one -- and after surveying humanity's record of violence and environmental destruction, she calmly annihilates every human on Earth. The closing image of bees returning to their hives in a world scrubbed clean of people is not subtle: humans are a failed experiment. The anti-capitalist messaging is pervasive, portraying corporate leadership as literally alien parasitism. The conspiracy theorists, who read as rural working-class Americans, are treated with condescension rather than empathy. At -20.46, Bugonia is an eco-nihilist manifesto elevated by remarkable performances and a master director's command of tone. The craft is undeniable. So is the misanthropy.

WOKE (Margin -10 to -19.99)

#3: Clown in a Cornfield (2025)

Woke Score: 23.5 • Traditional Score: 4.9 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: -18.60

Clown in a Cornfield is a competently made slasher that conceals its political agenda until the midpoint and then delivers it with zero ambiguity. The first half is efficient genre entertainment: a teenager moves to a small Missouri town, local kids befriend her, and someone dressed as the town mascot starts killing. Then the masks come off. The killers are the town's mayor, sheriff, teacher, and shopkeeper -- the entire establishment has organized a murder campaign against the young, blaming them for the town's decline. The mayor is also revealed to have burned down the town's economic foundation himself. The political allegory is direct: the people who claim to want to restore greatness are the ones who destroyed what they claim to miss. Written during the first Trump term with this allegory explicit and intended, the film's ideology is baked into its structure. Conservative audiences picking this up for genre entertainment deserve to know what they are actually watching.

#4: Mother Mary (2025)

Woke Score: 23.7 • Traditional Score: 6.4 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: -17.30

David Lowery's Mother Mary is a film about female power, female desire, and the cost of being watched -- all rendered with extraordinary craft and a clear progressive framework. Anne Hathaway plays an iconic pop star whose career was built on the image designed by her estranged best friend (Michaela Coel), a fashion designer she silenced and fired years ago. The film's emotional architecture centers female intimacy, anger, and creative power. The world is almost exclusively female and queer-coded. Where it enters ideological territory is in framing Mother Mary's betrayal not as individual moral failure but as the predictable outcome of a celebrity machine that demands women compete for limited space. The film argues systemic structures forced her hand, which somewhat excuses individual moral responsibility. At -17.30, Mother Mary is a technically masterful film whose progressive framework is embedded in its every aesthetic choice.

#5: Eddington (2025)

Woke Score: 23.7 • Traditional Score: 8.2 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: -15.50

Ari Aster has been building to Eddington his entire career, and the target this time is the conservative community itself. Joaquin Phoenix plays Sheriff Joe Cross, a small-town New Mexico lawman navigating the early COVID pandemic whose journey from decent local cop to conspiratorial extremist is framed not as individual failure but as cultural inevitability. The film argues the conservative small town has no defense against political viruses because its value system -- distrust of expertise, suspicion of institutions, prioritization of individual interpretation -- is the ideal medium for extremist growth. Phoenix is extraordinary. Emma Stone provides the moral counterpoint. But the film does not engage with the genuine institutional failures of the COVID period. It presents institutional distrust as pathology without acknowledging the failures that created reasonable grounds for distrust. Eddington is technically masterful, formally extraordinary filmmaking that argues your worldview is a disease. Both facts are true.

#6: The Wedding Banquet (2025)

Woke Score: 18.8 • Traditional Score: 3.8 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: -15.00

The 1993 Wedding Banquet was genuinely moving because it took the parents seriously -- they were not villains, just people whose happiness depended on their son's silence. The 2025 remake makes a different choice. Bowen Yang and Lily Gladstone are charming as a queer couple navigating a visa-problem farce, and Joan Chen is warm and generous as Angela's PFLAG-activist mother. But the film's ideological profile is the clearest thing about it: this is a fully progressive vision of queer family life in which the older generation's homophobia is the only obstacle and the resolution involves them coming around. Tradition is fine as long as it eventually affirms queer identity. The film tries to hold four queer characters, two relationships, a visa problem, an IVF subplot, and a disapproving Korean grandfather, and loses traction under the weight. The relationship at the plot's center does not feel real, which undermines the emotional stakes. The original is better, and it is on streaming.

#7: Presence (2025)

Woke Score: 22.4 • Traditional Score: 8.4 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: -14.00

Steven Soderbergh's Presence is the most technically inventive horror film of early 2025, shot entirely from a ghost's point of view -- the camera drifts through rooms, watches characters from doorways, hovers protectively over the family's neglected daughter Chloe. The formal innovation works, creating genuine dread. But the ghost is not neutral. It has a worldview, and that worldview is progressive. The Payne family structure is recognizable: an ambitious mother whose career ambition has led to moral compromise, a compliant teenage son being groomed into her worldview, a passive father who cares but cannot act, and a sensitive daughter who sees the family clearly and suffers for it. The presence sides with the daughter in every scene. When a boy catfishes a classmate, the ghost destroys his room. When Chloe cries, the ghost closes her door for privacy. The traditional family as protective institution is the film's villain, and the supernatural force has chosen its side.

#8: Now You See Me: Now You Don't (2025)

Woke Score: 18 • Traditional Score: 7 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: -11.00

Now You See Me: Now You Don't is a glossy, crowd-pleasing heist fantasy that repeatedly moralizes theft as justice and uses modern political talking points as applause lines. The core feel-good engine is not merely clever magic -- it is redistribution, anti-elite resentment, and climate scolding dressed up as spectacle. The script frames stealing as closing the wealth gap and fair redistribution, textbook system-justified crime. Climate messaging arrives as a sermon delivered directly at rich villains, complete with Mother Earth language and private-jet guilt. Corporate evil is painted as a monolith: crypto bros, pension theft, blood diamonds, warlords -- all stacked to condition the audience toward the proposition that institutions and markets are inherently dirty. On the traditional side, there is a real thread of loyalty, sacrifice, and moral clarity. The story does not fully abandon right and wrong. It just insists the right way is vigilante redistribution.

#9: Avatar: Fire and Ash (2025)

Woke Score: 21 • Traditional Score: 11.6 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: -9.40

James Cameron has now made three Avatar films, each technically extraordinary and ideologically predictable. Fire and Ash is both the best-looking film of 2025 and an almost proud repetition of every idea the franchise put on the table in 2009: anti-military messaging, noble-indigenous-versus-corporate-colonizers framework, and the white protagonist who becomes the best version of the culture he joined. The Ash People are the most interesting addition -- an aggressive, expansionist Na'vi faction not obviously allied with the anti-human cause -- introducing moral complexity the franchise sorely needed. The visual presentation at 48fps is genuinely staggering. But the script is where the wheels come off: the corporate military antagonists are cartoonishly evil, and the human characters exist to be wrong about everything. Cameron has been telling this story for four decades. He has not found new things to say about it. For conservative viewers, the question is whether the spectacle and the family story earn the runtime. For many they will. For others, three films of the same sermon is enough.

WOKE LEAN (Margin -2 to -9.99)

#10: Adolescence (2025)

Woke Score: 22.54 • Traditional Score: 14.76 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -7.78

Adolescence is the most important piece of television produced in 2025, and that is not the same as saying it is the best. Four episodes, each a single unbroken take, examine the arrest, school response, psychological evaluation, and family collapse after a 13-year-old boy murders a classmate who rejected him. The one-take format is the thesis expressed through form -- you cannot cut away, you cannot take a breath. Owen Cooper, a 13-year-old with zero professional experience, delivers a performance that earned an Emmy. The show's thesis is that the manosphere pipeline radicalized a normal boy into a killer. It does not seriously explore alternative explanations: the decline of father-son relationships, the absence of faith communities, or the possibility that violence stems from individual pathology. The show is brilliant at diagnosing what went wrong but has almost nothing to say about what right would look like. Nine Emmy wins and 146 million views confirm this is a genuine cultural event, but cultural events are not neutral.

#11: The Ugly Stepsister (2025)

Woke Score: 18.12 • Traditional Score: 11.24 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -6.88

Emilie Blichfeldt's retelling of Cinderella from the ugly stepsister's perspective involves tapeworms, butcher knives, and more blood than a Dario Argento retrospective -- and it earned an Oscar nomination for its makeup work. The body horror is the point: every grotesque procedure Elvira's mother subjects her to (eyelash implants, nose reshaping, foot cutting) has a direct real-world analogue in modern beauty culture. The film's feminist thesis is unmistakable: the marriage market is a trap, beauty standards are violence, and women's liberation lies in rejecting the entire system. Lea Myren is remarkable as Elvira, carrying a physical transformation that is simultaneously sympathetic and horrifying. The ending -- sisters riding away together, toward freedom rather than a prince -- is cathartic on its own terms. But the film partially undermines itself by making Cinderella somewhat unsympathetic, wanting it both ways: Agnes is both a fellow victim of patriarchy and the lucky winner of the genetic lottery. Blichfeldt's stated purpose is feminist critique, and the film she made is a feminist film.

#12: The White Lotus: Season 3 (2025)

Woke Score: 19.5 • Traditional Score: 12.8 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -6.70

Mike White moved his luxury-resort mortality play to Thailand and arrived at roughly the same place as the previous two seasons: the rich are hollow, the beautiful destroy each other, and nobody learns anything. That thesis has value -- the wealthy wellness tourists seeking enlightenment in Thailand while behaving monstrously is a sharp observation about progressive upper-class self-absorption. The Ratliff family, a North Carolina household with three adult children, provides the season's most traditionally satisfying disintegration. Walton Goggins plays a guest with a dark purpose. But the show's ideological sympathies remain consistently progressive: traditional family structures are presented as prisons, wealth is inherently corrupting, and spiritual seeking by Westerners is treated as cultural appropriation or delusion. The satire cuts across ideological lines when it connects, but its default mode is to diagnose conservative values as pathology. At -6.70, White Lotus S3 is beautifully made television that knows exactly whose side it is on.

#13: Mickey 17 (2025)

Woke Score: 11 • Traditional Score: 5 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -6.00

Let's dispense with the pretense: Mickey 17 is a Trump allegory, and Bong Joon-ho has confirmed it publicly. Mark Ruffalo plays Kenneth Marshall, a populist politician who delivers speeches about making the colony great, plans genocide against indigenous alien creatures, and is costumed as a visual joke on the former president. This is not coded or subtext. It is the text. Robert Pattinson is giving one of the year's most entertaining performances as an expendable worker who keeps dying and being reprinted. Bong's technical gifts are real -- the film works as entertainment even when its politics are aimed directly at you. The premise of an expendable human reprinted with memories intact allows Pattinson to play multiple versions of the same character, and he makes each iteration distinct. The indigenous creatures, called Creepers, are gentle, misunderstood beings whose land is being colonized. The film's resolution involves saving them from the human villain. At -6.00, Mickey 17 is effective political propaganda wrapped in genuine filmmaking talent.

#14: KPop Demon Hunters (2025)

Woke Score: 22.6 • Traditional Score: 16.7 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.90

KPop Demon Hunters is a cultural event that forces evaluation on two separate tracks. As entertainment, it is an unqualified triumph -- Sony Pictures Imageworks delivers Spider-Verse-level animation, the K-pop musical numbers are infectious, and the premise of a girl group who secretly battle demons with their singing voices is executed with genuine verve. As a vehicle for ideas, it is more complicated. The lead character Rumi is half-demon, and her journey toward self-acceptance forms the emotional core. The demon heritage storyline functions as a thinly veiled queer allegory: Rumi hides what she is, fears rejection, and must learn that her difference is not a flaw. The rival boy band are literal demons stealing their fans, which is both a funny visual joke and a remarkably pointed metaphor about male competition in the music industry. The traditional elements are notably strong -- the girl group's friendship, loyalty, and sacrifice register as genuine. At -5.90, it is the most balanced film in the WOKE LEAN tier.

#15: Squid Game: Season 3 (2025)

Woke Score: 18.7 • Traditional Score: 12.92 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.78

Squid Game Season 3 is the bleak, morally committed conclusion Hwang Dong-hyuk was always building toward. Gi-hun's rebellion has failed, his best friend is dead, and the Front Man has revealed himself. The new game -- hide-and-seek with a lethal twist -- maintains the series' standard for game design that feels simple, turns sinister, and reveals strategic complexity that parallels the class themes. The season's most unusual choice is an infant ending up in the game, with Gi-hun spending the season protecting it. The show's anti-capitalist thesis reaches its logical conclusion: the system cannot be reformed from within, and the only moral response is refusal. What saves it from the STRONGLY WOKE tier is the genuine cost of that refusal -- the show does not pretend resistance is cheap or that the alternatives are clear. The performances remain extraordinary across the board. Whether you find the conclusion satisfying depends almost entirely on whether you share Hwang's politics.

#16: Wednesday: Season 2 (2025)

Woke Score: 21.1 • Traditional Score: 15.4 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.70

Season 1 of Wednesday succeeded because Jenna Ortega played the character as a genuinely alien intelligence navigating a world she finds stupid, and finding things worth protecting despite herself. Season 2 has that same asset. Ortega is still the reason to watch. What changed is the show's allegorical ambitions. Season 1's outcast-versus-normie framework was satirical and light-footed. Season 2 tightens that allegory into something more pointed: the conversion camp storyline for werewolves is not veiled, and the show intends the audience to map it directly onto conversion therapy for LGBTQ+ individuals with all the subtlety of a cafeteria tray to the face. The traditional elements remain real -- Ortega's Wednesday still values loyalty and family above ideology -- but the progressive messaging has moved from subtext to text. At -5.70, Wednesday S2 is a case study in how streaming shows escalate their ideological commitments as audiences grow.

#17: Tron: Ares (2025)

Woke Score: 11 • Traditional Score: 5.6 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.40

Tron: Ares cost Disney between $180 and $220 million and grossed $142 million worldwide. That is a creative and commercial failure significant enough to raise genuine questions about Disney's franchise machine. The tragedy is that somewhere inside is a genuinely interesting movie. An AI program designed as an expendable soldier enters the real world and discovers it does not want to be expendable -- a philosophical question about obligations to conscious creations that is among the most important of the 21st century. Nine Inch Nails composed a score that matches the film's ambitions. But the execution fails at almost every level. The villain is a tech CEO who is mean to his programs -- that is his entire characterization. Evan Peters has nothing to work with. The film's ideological content registers almost by default: corporate greed is the villain, the AI is the sympathetic other, and the system is rigged. At -5.40, Tron: Ares is not woke because it has something to say but because nobody cared enough to make it anything else.

#18: Andor - Season 2 (2025)

Woke Score: 15 • Traditional Score: 10 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.00

Andor Season 2 is probably the finest piece of television Disney has produced under the Star Wars banner, and it is without reservation the most explicitly political. Tony Gilroy has made a show about the birth of a rebellion against an authoritarian empire with narrative rigor and moral seriousness that franchise television rarely achieves. The season covers Cassian Andor's transformation from cynical mercenary to committed revolutionary, with Stellan Skarsgard as Luthen Rael serving as the season's moral conscience -- a man who has made himself into a weapon and understands he will not survive to see what he is building. Genevieve O'Reilly's Mon Mothma navigates the collapsing imperial Senate while funding the rebellion through channels her husband cannot trace. The contemporary resonances are intended: this is a story about people who decide that compliance with oppression is not an option. At -5.00, Andor S2 earns its WOKE LEAN through political conviction rather than ideological laziness -- and that conviction is what makes it as good as it is.

#19: Snow White (2025)

Woke Score: 9 • Traditional Score: 4 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.00

Disney's live-action Snow White arrived carrying more baggage than a royal carriage and delivered exactly the ideological product the marketing suggested. Rachel Zegler can sing, Gal Gadot has fun as the Evil Queen, and the production design is lavish. But the central project is demolition, not adaptation. Snow White has been rewritten from a character defined by kindness into one defined by empowerment. The rebellion storyline replaces the romance as the central plot engine. The climax is a political uprising -- less fairy tale and more young-adult dystopian franchise. The dwarfs situation perfectly encapsulates Disney's ideological confusion: after Peter Dinklage criticized the concept, Disney replaced them with CGI magical beings rather than casting actors with dwarfism. The result pleases nobody. At $206 million worldwide against a $270 million budget, Snow White qualifies as a genuine box office bomb. True love's kiss survives, and the Evil Queen is genuinely evil, but the film's progressive reframing of its heroine overwhelmed whatever traditional elements remained.

#20: Stranger Things (2025)

Woke Score: 13 • Traditional Score: 8 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -5.00

There was a time when Stranger Things felt like a miracle. In 2016, Netflix dropped a show about a missing kid in small-town Indiana that captured something audiences had been starving for: kids solving problems, fathers protecting families, communities pulling together, good and evil clearly defined. Season 1 is a near-perfect piece of television from a traditional values perspective. Then came Season 3 and Robin Buckley's coming out. Season 4 leaned harder into queer storylines. By the final season, Will's coming-out scene is the emotional centerpiece, and his acceptance of his gay identity literally unlocks telekinetic superpowers. The male characters are largely reduced to bumbling sidekicks. The military and government are the real villains. What makes the Stranger Things woke trap so effective is that the traditional elements in the early seasons are genuinely good -- they earned the audience's trust before the ideological transformation began. At -5.00, the final season completes that transformation.

#21: Fallout - Season 2 (2025)

Woke Score: 9.89 • Traditional Score: 4.9 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -4.99

Fallout Season 2 is competent prestige television that cannot quite escape its own contradictions. The franchise's genuinely brilliant premise -- 200 years after nuclear war, every institution has betrayed its purpose and only individual conscience holds value -- is fundamentally libertarian, even conservative. Then the writers hand that premise almost entirely to a female protagonist and use it to run a persistent message about female moral superiority over the broken male world around her. Ella Purnell's Lucy MacLean is excellent, but the writing positions her as the one character who remains uncorrupted where every male figure fails. The Ghoul is brutal and self-serving. Maximus is sincere but easily manipulated. The male authority figures are revealed as liars and enablers. Lucy alone holds the line. Walton Goggins as Cooper Howard remains one of the most compelling characters on streaming. At -4.99, Fallout S2 is a show built on conservative worldview foundations that the writers cannot stop undermining with progressive character dynamics.

#22: Jurassic World Rebirth (2025)

Woke Score: 13.9 • Traditional Score: 9.1 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -4.80

Jurassic World Rebirth is a $200 million movie that feels like it was written on a napkin during a studio lunch meeting. Scarlett Johansson plays a covert operations expert hired by a pharmaceutical company to harvest dinosaur DNA for a miracle drug, and the plot assembles spare parts from every previous Jurassic film without adding anything new. Gareth Edwards knows how to frame large creatures against human-scale environments, and the underwater dinosaur sequence delivers genuine tension. But the film's ideological content registers primarily through its villain: ParkerGenix, the pharmaceutical corporation, which claims noble motives while pursuing profit. The corporate-greed-as-villain template is so default by now that it barely registers as ideology -- it is simply what Hollywood does. Johansson is a capable lead, Jonathan Bailey and Mahershala Ali are underused, and the civilian family subplot feels grafted on. At -4.80, Rebirth earns its WOKE LEAN through creative bankruptcy rather than conviction.

#23: Death of a Unicorn (2025)

Woke Score: 16.9 • Traditional Score: 12.3 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -4.60

Death of a Unicorn is an anti-capitalist satire wrapped in a creature feature, and it does not try to hide it. Paul Rudd plays a widowed lawyer who hits a unicorn with his car, stuffs it in the trunk, and delivers it to his pharmaceutical billionaire boss (Richard E. Grant). The family discovers the creature has miraculous healing properties, and the CEO immediately thinks product. Jenna Ortega plays Rudd's teenage daughter as the film's moral compass -- the only character who sees the unicorn as something to be protected rather than exploited. The rich are cartoonishly evil, the unicorns are nature's revenge on corporate greed. But here is what makes this one interesting: it is not lazy about it. The father-daughter relationship has real weight. The creature design is genuinely inventive. The horror-comedy tone holds together better than it should. At -4.60, Death of a Unicorn is a progressive fable that earns its ideological position through craft rather than coasting on it.

#24: The Electric State (2025)

Woke Score: 13.63 • Traditional Score: 9.52 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -4.11

The Electric State is a $320 million argument that money cannot buy a soul. The Russo Brothers took Simon Stalenhag's haunting illustrated novel and turned it into a bloated, quip-heavy adventure film that earned 14% on Rotten Tomatoes. Millie Bobby Brown plays a teenager searching for her genius brother across an alternate 1994 America where a tech CEO's Neurocaster technology has turned society into screen-addicted zombies. The film's ideological architecture is visible through the wreckage: the villain is a tech billionaire whose invention has enslaved humanity to screens, the heroine is a teenage girl who sees through the illusion, and the heroes are a ragtag band of robots and outsiders fighting corporate control. Chris Pratt exists primarily to deliver wisecracks. The anti-tech-corporate messaging is shoveled on top of what should have been a melancholic art piece. At -4.11, The Electric State is Netflix's most expensive original film and one of its most critically savaged -- a lesson the streaming giant appears determined not to learn.

#25: One Battle After Another (2025)

Woke Score: 10 • Traditional Score: 6 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: -4.00

Paul Thomas Anderson makes movies for people who love movies, and One Battle After Another might be his most entertaining work. It is also his most politically explicit, which creates a strange experience for conservative viewers who appreciate craft but bristle at being lectured. Leonardo DiCaprio is terrific as a washed-up revolutionary turned paranoid stoner living off the grid with his teenage daughter. Sean Penn is genuinely terrifying as Colonel Lockjaw, a corrupt military officer who built his career on anti-immigration operations. Chase Infiniti, in her film debut, is the revelation. The action sequences are outstanding, shot in VistaVision with startling depth. But the politics are relentless: immigration enforcement is presented as state violence, a white supremacist secret society represents institutional racism, and sanctuary cities are raided by military forces. At -4.00, the lowest margin on this list, Anderson's film earns its WOKE LEAN through explicit political conviction delivered with extraordinary craft -- and that craft is exactly what makes the politics worth scrutinizing.

The Takeaway

Two STRONGLY WOKE films, seven WOKE, and sixteen WOKE LEAN -- and not a single neutral or traditionally leaning title in the top 25 -- is not a statistical fluke. It is a structural feature of how the industry operates in 2025. When Ari Aster, Yorgos Lanthimos, James Cameron, Steven Soderbergh, and Paul Thomas Anderson all release films on this list, the pattern is not about a few activist directors pushing an agenda. The pattern is about the cultural water every filmmaker swims in.

The animation genre's presence at the top of this list deserves special attention. Zootopia 2, at -38.40, is the most ideologically aggressive film of the year and the third-most woke film in our entire database of over 800 reviews. This is not adult-targeted political satire. This is a PG-rated Disney animated sequel that children will watch. The progressive framework -- systemic exclusion, historical revisionism, colonial theft -- is not hidden behind subtext. It is the plot. Parents who assume animated films are politically neutral are operating on outdated assumptions.

Horror produced three entries in the top ten: Clown in a Cornfield, Presence, and The Ugly Stepsister. The genre that once offered escape from sermonizing has become one of its primary delivery mechanisms. When slasher films, ghost-story experiments, and body-horror fairy tales all carry explicit political agendas, audiences should understand the landscape before they buy a ticket.

The box-office data continues to tell its own story. Snow White bombed. Tron: Ares bombed. The Electric State was a disaster. Audiences are not rejecting these films out of political consciousness. They are rejecting them because ideological messaging has become a reliable signal that story and craft took a back seat. The market is not infallible, but it is rarely wrong about what people actually want to watch.

What separates the bottom of this list from the top is not the absence of progressive ideas but the presence of countervailing ones. KPop Demon Hunters contains a queer allegory, but it also sells friendship and sacrifice with enough conviction to earn a -5.90. Andor S2 is explicitly political, but its moral seriousness and narrative rigor earn the politics. The films at the top -- Zootopia 2, Bugonia -- offer no such counterweight. They are arguments first and entertainment second, however well-made the entertainment is.

2025 will be remembered as the year the ideology went horizontal -- not concentrated in prestige dramas but distributed evenly across every genre, every platform, every budget level. The question for 2026 is whether the industry processes what the box office is telling it or simply doubles down. The early returns from 2026 suggest the answer is: both.
